title: Noise-Power Trade-Off and Noise Bandwidth
intro: Input-referred thermal noise falls as $1/g_m$, so lower noise costs current. And total noise depends on how much bandwidth the circuit integrates, which the noise bandwidth makes comparable between circuits.

blocks.text: Take a CS stage, double $W/L$ and $I_D$ and halve $R_D$. Gain and swings are unchanged, but $g_m$ and the gate area double, so the input thermal and flicker noise powers halve: 3 dB less noise for twice the power (and twice the input capacitance). It is the same as placing two copies of the circuit in parallel.
In general, two identical circuits in parallel each see the other's output impedance as a divider of 1/2, so

This assumes the bandwidth is fixed by the application, and that the input noise current is negligible: scaling doubles $\overline{I_{n,in}^2}$, because the input impedance halves. Input-referred noise power times supply power is therefore roughly constant for a topology at given bandwidth.
At fixed overdrive, doubling $g_m$ means doubling current and width; at fixed $W/L$ it would take four times the current, since $g_m \propto \sqrt{I_D}$.

Total noise is the area under the output spectrum, including the tail beyond the $-3$ dB point. The noise bandwidth $B_n$ is defined so that a flat spectrum at the low-frequency level $V_0^2$, cut off sharply at $B_n$, has the same area:

blocks.alt: Normalised one-pole noise spectrum against frequency over pole frequency, falling to one half at fp; a shaded rectangle of height one extends to pi over two times fp and has the same area as the curve.
blocks.caption: Equal areas define the noise bandwidth.

blocks.text: For two identical poles $B_n = (\pi/4)f_p$, while the $-3$ dB bandwidth is $0.64f_p$: the ratio of noise to $-3$ dB bandwidth shrinks as roll-off steepens (1.57 for one pole, 1.22 for two). $B_n$ lets you compare circuits with the same low-frequency noise but different high-frequency behaviour.
Integrate at the output, not the input

Input-referred noise is often flat (the CS stage's $4kT\gamma/g_m$), and integrating it over all frequencies would give infinity. Only the output noise, which the circuit's poles shape, integrates to a finite value. For a fair comparison, integrate at the output and divide by the square of the mid-band gain. blocks.title: Integrated noise
blocks.text: White noise of $10\text{ nV}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ passes through a one-pole low-pass filter with its pole at 1 MHz. Find the total rms output noise.

blocks.title: Paying for 6 dB
blocks.text: An amplifier draws 2 mA and has $3\text{ nV}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ input noise (thermal, negligible noise current). By linear scaling, what current gives $1.5\text{ nV}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$?
solution: Halving the voltage density means a quarter of the noise power: two doublings of the scaling.
Each doubling doubles the current: $2\text{ mA} \times 4 = 8\text{ mA}$.

blocks.text: A current-source-loaded CS stage has $g_m = 4\text{ mS}$, $R_D = 5\text{ k}\Omega$ (output resistance), $C_L = 1\text{ pF}$ and $\gamma = 1$. Ignoring load noise, find the total input-referred rms noise.
